sections.section_title: Paul's Second Visit to Jerusalem -- Timing, Companions, and Revelation
sections.summary: Paul narrates his second visit to Jerusalem after fourteen years, undertaken because of a divine revelation, to present his law-free gospel to the recognized leaders privately.

sections.section_title: The Titus Test Case -- Circumcision Refused
sections.summary: Titus, an uncircumcised Greek believer, was not compelled to be circumcised by the Jerusalem leadership, and Paul refused to yield to false brothers who sought to impose Torah observance on Gentile believers.

sections.section_title: The Jerusalem Pillars Add Nothing -- Mutual Recognition
sections.summary: The Jerusalem pillars -- James, Cephas, and John -- added nothing to Paul's gospel, recognized his divine commission to the Gentiles as parallel to Peter's commission to the Jews, and extended the right hand of fellowship.

Paul publicly confronted Cephas in Antioch for withdrawing from Gentile table fellowship under pressure from the circumcision party, exposing the hypocrisy of a Jew who had been living like a Gentile now compelling Gentiles to live like Jews.

sections.section_title: The Theological Turn -- Justification by Faith, Not Works of Law
sections.summary: Paul argues that even Jews by birth recognized that justification comes through faith in Jesus Christ, not through works of the law, and therefore they themselves believed in Christ.
sections.relevance: The passage presents believing as a genuine human act undertaken by Jewish believers who recognized Torah's insufficiency: 'we also have believed in Christ Jesus, in order to be justified by faith in Christ.' The verb episteusamen ('we believed') frames faith as something these individuals did -- they recognized, they believed, they acted. The primary argument is about the instrument of justification (faith vs. Torah observance), not about who determines salvation outcomes, but the passage's consistent presentation of faith as a real human response has clear implications for human agency.
key_phrases: we know that a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ
so we also have believed in Christ Jesus, in order to be justified by faith in Christ
by works of the law no one will be justified

sections.section_title: The Absurdity of Rebuilding What Was Torn Down
sections.summary: Paul argues that returning to Torah observance after embracing justification in Christ would make him a transgressor by rebuilding the very system he demolished, directly implicating Cephas's withdrawal from Gentile fellowship.

sections.section_title: Death to the Law, Life to God
sections.summary: Paul describes dying to the law through the law so as to live to God, having been crucified with Christ so that Christ now lives in him, while the life he continues to live in the flesh is lived by faith in the Son of God.
sections.relevance: The passage holds divine action and human agency in active tension. 'Christ lives in me' presents the indwelling Christ as the animating principle of Paul's new existence, but the neutral reading clarifies this is 'not mystical annihilation of personhood.' Paul immediately adds 'the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith' -- presenting his ongoing faith as his own genuine activity. The result is a picture in which divine presence empowers rather than replaces human agency: Christ indwells, and Paul believes. Faith remains a real human activity even within a life transformed by divine action.
key_phrases: I have been crucified with Christ
it is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me
the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God
who loved me and gave himself for me

sections.section_title: The Conclusion -- Grace Stands or Falls
sections.summary: Paul concludes that he does not nullify the grace of God, since if righteousness could come through the law, then Christ died for no purpose -- framing the choice as between grace in Christ and Torah-based righteousness.
